At 4:17 every morning, the town’s clocks stopped.

Not all at once. The clock above the bakery would shudder first, its brass hands trembling over the painted number eight. Then the station clock, which had been ten minutes fast since anyone could remember, would click backward. The church clock would lose its minute hand entirely. Digital displays went dark. Phones showed a blank gray square where the time should have been.

For sixty seconds, the town existed without an hour.

People learned not to speak during that minute. Children were told it was when the dead came home, though no one could say who had started the story. The baker claimed he had once heard footsteps crossing his kitchen. The stationmaster insisted someone had knocked three times on the locked office door. Old Mrs. Vale said the dead had better manners than that.

Mara did not believe in the dead.

She believed in loose wires, failing batteries, atmospheric disturbances, and the general unreliability of human memory. She repaired clocks for a living, which meant she spent her days arguing with time and her evenings losing.

Her father had taught her the trade. He used to say that every clock was a small, stubborn animal: if you listened carefully, it would tell you what hurt.

“Most problems are simple,” he’d say, leaning close to a mechanism. “A bent tooth. A tired spring. Dust in the wrong place.”

“What about people?” Mara had asked once.

He had looked at her over his spectacles. “People are clocks that learned to lie.”

He died in February, during a rainstorm that lasted three days. Afterward, Mara found a note in his workshop, tucked inside the wooden case of an unfinished clock.

At 4:17. Come alone.

That was all.

She kept the note for six months before deciding it was either meaningless or meant for someone else. Then, on a cold morning in September, she woke at 4:12 with the certainty that someone was standing beside her bed.

No one was there.

At 4:16, she dressed.

The town was silent when she stepped outside. Even the river seemed to be holding its breath. She walked to the workshop, unlocked the door, and sat beneath the largest clock her father had ever built. It had no hands. Its face was a circle of dark wood, polished until it reflected nothing.

At 4:17, every clock stopped.

The sound was not silence. Silence was soft. This was a vast suspension, as though the world had become a photograph.

Then the clock above Mara began to tick.

Once.

Twice.

A panel opened in its base.

Inside was a narrow staircase descending into darkness.

Mara thought of her father’s voice. A clock, he had said, was a small, stubborn animal.

She took a lantern and went down.

The stairs ended beneath the town.

There was a room there, larger than any room had the right to be. Its walls were covered in clocks: round clocks, square clocks, clocks shaped like birds and moons and open hands. Some were no bigger than buttons. Others were tall as trees. All of them had stopped at 4:17.

In the center stood a table.

On it lay a single object: a pocket watch.

Mara picked it up.

The watch opened by itself.

Inside the lid was a photograph of her father, young and smiling beside a woman Mara had never seen. The woman had Mara’s eyes.

Behind the photograph, written in her father’s careful hand, were the words:

Your mother is not dead.

Mara sat down.

For a long time, nothing moved. Then one of the clocks on the wall began to tick. A small silver one. Its hands advanced by a single minute.

4:18.

The room changed.

A door appeared in the far wall.

Mara stood, though her knees were shaking, and crossed toward it. Before she touched the handle, she heard music on the other side: a lullaby her father had hummed whenever he thought she was asleep.

She opened the door.

Beyond it was the town, but not as it was now. The streets were bright with summer. The river ran backward. People moved like shadows beneath water. At the end of the road, a woman stood beneath an apple tree.

Mara knew her immediately.

Not from memory. From the shape of her face, which was the shape of Mara’s own face before grief had changed it.

The woman lifted one hand.

Mara stepped through.

Behind her, somewhere far away, every clock in town began ticking again.

The minute returned to the world.

But Mara did not.

And from that morning on, people noticed a new thing. At 4:17, when the clocks stopped, a woman could sometimes be seen walking along the riverbank, carrying a lantern. Beside her walked another woman, older and slower, holding a pocket watch between them.

They never spoke.

They only walked until the minute ended.

Then, together, they disappeared.
